title: Stroke Sorter

source.quote: A stroke is defined as a unit of recognition.

setting: Tuesday, 7 a.m. opening shift at the diner. Rosita's run this floor for six years. The lines keep coming - she's sorting what people throw at her faster than she can respond to it.

L1.line: Table six says the eggs were perfect again. You trained them well.
cues: about what she did (training the staff), not about who she is
L1.question: Rosita gets this over the pass window mid-rush. What kind of stroke is it?

options.text: Positive, unconditional - warm, and about who she is, not anything she did.
options.feedback: Unconditional would be about who she is ("you're great"), not what she did. This one's tied to the training, so it's conditional.

options.text: Positive, conditional - pleasant to hear, and tied to a specific thing she did.
options.feedback: Right - it's positive (pleasant to receive) and conditional (tied to a specific thing she did: training the staff).

options.text: Negative, conditional - painful to hear, tied to something she did.
options.feedback: Negative strokes feel painful to the receiver. This one's warm and complimentary - it's positive, not negative.

options.text: Negative, unconditional - painful to hear, aimed at who she is.
options.feedback: Neither negative nor unconditional fits - it's warm (positive) and tied to a specific action (conditional).

L1.lesson: Positive/negative is about how a stroke feels to receive; conditional/unconditional is about whether it's tied to what you did or to who you are. The two axes are independent - this one lands as positive and conditional.

L2.intro: The rush doesn't stop for sorting. Three more strokes come at Rosita before 8am - and the real skill isn't naming them, it's deciding what to do with each one.

cues: same compliment as before - now it's Rosita's move to respond

options.text: Say "thanks, I'll take that" and actually let it land.
options.outcome: It sits with her. On the next sprint to table nine, she's a half-step lighter.
options.lesson: Taking in a stroke you agree with, instead of discounting it, is what tops up the stroke bank - a healthy stroke quotient only works if you actually accept the strokes that fit.

options.text: Say "eh, they're easy tables, not me."
options.outcome: Dev shrugs. "Sure, whatever you say." The compliment doesn't stick - it never got taken in.
options.lesson: This is the stroke filter in action - discounting a positive that doesn't match how Rosita sees herself, even though nothing about the stroke was dishonest.

options.text: Say nothing and grab the next ticket.
options.outcome: Dev doesn't push it a second time. Rosita stays stroke-hungry and doesn't notice why.
options.lesson: Ignoring a stroke isn't neutral - it's a quiet way of staying in a familiar deficit instead of letting in something that might shift how she sees herself.

beats.line: You're always so slow at this counter.
cues: said flat, phone already in hand

options.text: Ask: "Was today specifically slow, or is this a general thing?"
options.outcome: Priya pauses. "I guess - just today, the register jammed." The real information comes out.
options.lesson: A straight negative gives you a signal you can act on; a discount like "always" distorts reality and gives you nothing to work with until you ask past it.

options.text: Apologize and promise to be faster from now on.
options.outcome: Priya nods, mollified. Rosita spends the rest of the shift rushing tables that didn't need rushing.
options.lesson: Accepting a discount at face value means acting on a distortion - she's now correcting a problem ("always slow") that was never accurately described.

options.text: Tell her "you're always so slow" is unfair.
options.outcome: Priya bristles. "Forget it." Nothing about the register gets fixed, and now there's a second tense moment on top of the first.
options.lesson: Matching a discount with a counter-accusation keeps the exchange going instead of asking the question that would surface the actual, useful information underneath it.

beats.npc: Camellia, training on her first week
beats.line: Oh my gosh, you're literally the BEST boss I've ever had, this place would fall apart without you!
cues: said loudly, to everyone in earshot
the exact line she used on the dishwasher yesterday
big gestures, not much eye contact

options.text: Say thanks warmly, but file it as enthusiasm, not evidence.
options.outcome: Rosita smiles, says thanks, and goes back to the floor - unchanged either way.
options.lesson: Over-the-top, indiscriminate praise is what's sometimes called marshmallow-throwing - you don't need to reject it, just not bank it the way you'd bank a specific, sincere stroke.

options.text: Take it fully to heart - she must really mean it.
options.outcome: It feels great for an hour. By lunch, Camellia's said the identical line to the dishwasher, and Rosita feels a little foolish.
options.lesson: Accepting every stroke at full value regardless of the source is the flip side of too tight a filter - a filter this loose lets in strokes that don't actually hold up.

options.text: Tell Camellia to stop being so fake.
options.outcome: Camellia goes quiet and stops complimenting anyone - including the times she actually means it.
options.lesson: Confronting enthusiasm as fake can shut down a new hire's genuine strokes along with the insincere ones - the better move is just not over-weighting it, not punishing her for it.

echo.setting: 24 hours later: a coworker in the elevator.
echo.shape: same four-way sort - accept it, deflect it, over-value it, or let it pass unanswered
